lessons.title: Routine Field Scouting and Record Keeping
lessons.body: Walk your sweet potato field at least twice a week, early in the morning when pests are active and dew helps you spot disease. Start scouting one week after planting. Use a simple notebook or a mobile app to record what you see. Divide your field into sectionsâsay, 10 rows by 10 plantsâand check 10 random plants per section. Look for yellowing leaves, holes, wilting, or insects. Common pests in Africa include sweet potato weevils, caterpillars, and aphids. Diseases like sweet potato virus disease cause yellow veins and stunted growth. Record the date, section, problem, and action taken. For example, if you find 5 out of 10 plants with aphids, write 'Aphids on 5 plants, sprayed neem oil 5ml/L.' Keep a monthly summary to track patterns. If you see more than 10% of plants affected, act immediately. Use a hoe to remove severely diseased plants and burn them away from the field. Also note weatherârain, drought, or strong windsâbecause it affects pest outbreaks. A simple rain gauge made from a tin can help measure rainfall. At the end of each week, review your notes and plan next steps. This habit prevents small problems from becoming total crop loss. Many farmers lose 30-50% of yield due to late detection. With consistent scouting, you can catch issues early and protect your harvest.

lessons.title: Pruning and Vine Management
lessons.body: Sweet potato vines grow fast and can smother each other if left unchecked. Pruning means cutting back excess vines to direct energy into roots. Start when vines are about 30 cm long, usually 4-6 weeks after planting. Use a sharp knife or secateurs. Remove weak, diseased, or overcrowded vines. Leave 3-4 main vines per plant. Cut them back to 20-30 cm from the base. Do not prune more than 30% of the vine at once, or you will stress the plant. In dry areas, prune less; in wet areas, prune more to prevent rot. Vine management also includes lifting vines that have rooted at nodesâthese 'daughter plants' compete for nutrients. Gently lift vines every two weeks and turn them back onto the ridge. This is called 'vine turning' and prevents rooting. In Africa, many farmers practice vine cutting for livestock feed. You can cut up to 20% of vines for fodder without reducing yield, as long as you leave the main stems. After pruning, apply a light dose of fertilizerâone matchbox of NPK 15-15-15 per plantâto help recovery. Keep records of pruning dates and amounts. Pruning improves air flow, reduces disease, and increases marketable roots by 15-25%. Do not prune after the plants start flowering, as this can reduce root bulking. Always prune in the morning when it's cool, and avoid pruning during flowering or drought stress.

lessons.title: Hilling and Ridge Maintenance
lessons.body: Ridges are the backbone of sweet potato farming. They keep roots from rotting and allow easy harvesting. Over time, rain and foot traffic flatten ridges. You must rebuild them every 3-4 weeks. Use a hoe to pull soil up from the furrows onto the ridge. Aim for ridges 30-40 cm high and 60-80 cm wide. This is called 'hilling' or 'earthing up'. Do it when the soil is moist but not waterlogged. Hilling covers exposed roots and prevents greening, which makes roots bitter. It also controls weeds. In sandy soils, ridges collapse faster, so check after every heavy rain. In clay soils, ridges hold shape longer but can waterlogâmake furrows deeper. For large fields, use a tractor-drawn ridger, but most smallholders use hand hoes. A good ridge has a flat top, not pointed, so vines can spread. If you see cracks in the ridge, fill them with soil to stop weevil entry. Weevils lay eggs in cracks. Also, repair ridges after harvesting any early roots. In Africa, some farmers use 'flat planting' instead of ridges, but ridges give 20-30% higher yield and better root shape. Hilling is hard workâdo it in the cool of the day. One person can hill about 0.1 hectare per day. After hilling, apply mulch like dry grass to conserve moisture and suppress weeds. Keep records of hilling dates and ridge condition. Well-maintained ridges mean bigger, straighter roots.

lessons.title: Detecting Nutrient Deficiencies Early
lessons.body: Nutrient deficiencies show up in leaves before they affect roots. Learn to read the signs. Nitrogen deficiency: older leaves turn yellow, starting from the tip and moving along the vein. Plants look stunted. Fix it by applying 50 kg/ha of urea or 2 handfuls of poultry manure per plant. Potassium deficiency: leaf edges turn brown and dry, especially on older leaves. Roots become small and poorly shaped. Apply 100 kg/ha of muriate of potash or wood ash (2 cups per plant). Phosphorus deficiency: leaves turn dark green with purple tints, and roots are stubby. Apply 50 kg/ha of triple superphosphate or bone meal. Magnesium deficiency: yellowing between veins on older leaves. Spray 2% Epsom salt solution (20 g per litre) every two weeks. Iron deficiency: young leaves turn yellow while veins stay green. Common in alkaline soils. Spray 0.5% ferrous sulphate. Zinc deficiency: small leaves with yellow spots. Spray 0.2% zinc sulphate. Always check soil pH firstâsweet potatoes prefer pH 5.5-6.5. If pH is wrong, nutrients get locked up. Use a simple soil test kit from an agro-dealer. Test every season. Also, look for patterns: deficiencies often appear in patches, not whole fields. If you see symptoms on more than 10% of plants, act immediately. Over-fertilizing can also cause problemsâtoo much nitrogen gives lots of leaves but few roots. Keep a notebook with dates, symptoms, and treatments. Early detection can save 30% of your yield.

lessons.title: Managing Growth to Prevent Cracking and Oversizing
lessons.body: Cracked or oversized sweet potatoes fetch low prices. Cracking happens when roots grow too fast after a dry spell followed by heavy rain or irrigation. To prevent this, keep soil moisture steady. Water every 7-10 days if no rain, giving about 25 mm each time. Use drip irrigation or a watering can. Mulch with dry grass to hold moisture. Oversizing occurs when plants stay in the ground too long. Harvest at the right time: most varieties are ready 3-5 months after planting. Check by digging one or two rootsâif they are 15-20 cm long and 5-8 cm wide, they are ready. Do not leave them longer than 6 months. For market, aim for roots 150-300 g each. To slow growth, reduce nitrogen fertilizer after 2 months. If you see roots cracking, harvest immediately and sell quickly. Also, avoid heavy tillage near roots. In Africa, many farmers lose 20-40% of roots to cracking. Another cause is uneven hillingâif ridges are too shallow, roots push out and crack. Keep ridges 30 cm high. If you want large roots for a specific market, space plants widerâ40 cm between plants instead of 30 cmâand harvest at 5 months. But for most markets, medium size is best. Record harvest dates and root sizes. If cracking is a recurring problem, switch to a variety like 'Tanzania' or 'Ejumula' that resists cracking. Always test-dig before full harvest.

lessons.title: Using Technology for Crop Monitoring
lessons.body: You don't need expensive tools to use technology. A basic mobile phone can help. Use free apps like 'Plantix' or 'Crop Diagnosis' to identify pests and diseases from photos. Take clear pictures of affected leaves and uploadâthe app suggests treatments. For record keeping, use 'Google Sheets' or a notebook app. Record planting date, variety, fertilizer, and harvest. Set reminders for scouting, hilling, and harvesting. If you have internet, join WhatsApp groups for sweet potato farmers to share alerts. For soil moisture, buy a cheap moisture meter (about $10) or use the 'feel method': squeeze soil in your handâif it crumbles, it's dry; if it holds shape, it's moist. For larger farms, consider a drone or satellite service. In Kenya and Nigeria, companies like 'Ujuzi Kilimo' provide soil testing and SMS advice for a small fee. You can also use a rain gauge made from a plastic bottle to measure rainfall. Keep a simple weather log. If you have a smartphone, use 'AccuWeather' to track rain. For pest traps, use yellow sticky traps (buy or make with yellow plastic and grease) to monitor aphids and whiteflies. Count insects weekly. If numbers rise, spray neem oil. Technology is a tool, not a replacement for walking your field. Use it to save time and spot trends. Share your data with extension officers for better advice. Start smallâone app, one notebookâand build from there.

quiz.q: How often should you scout your sweet potato field?
options: C) Only when you see problems
quiz.explanation: Regular scouting twice a week helps catch pests and diseases early.

quiz.q: What is a key sign of sweet potato virus disease?
options: A) Yellow veins and stunted growth
quiz.explanation: Sweet potato virus disease causes yellow veins and stunted growth.

quiz.q: When should you start pruning sweet potato vines?
options: B) When vines are 30 cm long
quiz.explanation: Pruning starts when vines are about 30 cm long, usually 4-6 weeks after planting.

quiz.q: How much vine can you safely remove during pruning?
quiz.explanation: Removing more than 30% of vines at once stresses the plant.

quiz.q: What is vine turning?
options: B) Lifting vines to prevent rooting at nodes
quiz.explanation: Vine turning means lifting vines so they don't root at nodes and compete for nutrients.

quiz.q: How often should you rebuild ridges?
quiz.explanation: Ridges flatten over time and need rebuilding every 3-4 weeks.

quiz.q: What is the ideal height for sweet potato ridges?
quiz.explanation: Ridges 30-40 cm high prevent waterlogging and allow good root growth.

quiz.q: Why is hilling important?
options: A) It makes the field look neat
B) It covers exposed roots and controls weeds
quiz.explanation: Hilling covers roots to prevent greening and also suppresses weeds.

quiz.q: Which nutrient deficiency causes yellowing of older leaves?
quiz.explanation: Nitrogen deficiency starts with yellowing of older leaves.

quiz.q: What is a sign of potassium deficiency in sweet potatoes?
options: D) Small leaves with yellow spots
quiz.explanation: Potassium deficiency causes leaf edges to turn brown and dry.

quiz.q: What is the preferred soil pH for sweet potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Sweet potatoes grow best at pH 5.5-6.5.

quiz.q: How can you treat magnesium deficiency?
quiz.explanation: A 2% Epsom salt spray corrects magnesium deficiency.

quiz.q: What causes cracked sweet potatoes?
options: B) Uneven moisture after dry spell
quiz.explanation: Cracking occurs when roots grow too fast after a dry spell followed by heavy rain.

quiz.q: When are most sweet potato varieties ready for harvest?
quiz.explanation: Most varieties mature 3-5 months after planting.

quiz.q: What is a good size for market sweet potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Roots of 150-300 g are ideal for most markets.

quiz.q: How can you reduce oversized roots?
quiz.explanation: Reducing nitrogen after 2 months slows growth and prevents oversizing.

quiz.q: Which app can help identify sweet potato pests?
quiz.explanation: Plantix is a free app that diagnoses crop problems from photos.

quiz.q: What is a cheap tool for monitoring soil moisture?
quiz.explanation: A basic moisture meter costs about $10 and helps decide when to water.

quiz.q: What does the 'feel method' test?
quiz.explanation: Squeezing soil in your hand indicates moisture level.

quiz.q: What is a yellow sticky trap used for?
quiz.explanation: Yellow sticky traps attract and catch flying insects for monitoring.

quiz.q: How often should you record field observations?
quiz.explanation: Recording every scouting visit helps track trends and make timely decisions.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find more than 10% of plants with pests?
quiz.explanation: Acting immediately prevents pests from spreading and causing major loss.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of pruning sweet potato vines?
quiz.explanation: Pruning directs energy to root growth, increasing marketable roots.

quiz.q: What should you do after hilling?
quiz.explanation: Mulching after hilling conserves moisture and suppresses weeds.

quiz.q: Which nutrient deficiency causes purple tints on leaves?
quiz.explanation: Phosphorus deficiency can cause dark green leaves with purple tints.

quiz.q: What is a sign of iron deficiency?
options: A) Yellow young leaves with green veins
quiz.explanation: Iron deficiency causes interveinal yellowing on young leaves.

quiz.q: How can you prevent cracking in sweet potatoes?
quiz.explanation: Steady moisture prevents rapid growth that leads to cracking.

quiz.q: What is a good spacing to produce larger roots?
quiz.explanation: Wider spacing of 40 cm allows roots to grow larger.

quiz.q: Which variety is known to resist cracking?
quiz.explanation: Varieties like Tanzania and Ejumula are more resistant to cracking.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of using technology in crop monitoring?
options: B) Save time and spot trends
quiz.explanation: Technology helps save time and identify patterns, but field walks are still essential.
